meta.title: Use and Maintenance of Herbarium Press in Pharmacognosy Laboratory

sections.purpose: To press and dry freshly collected plant specimens into flat, preserved forms suitable for mounting on herbarium sheets as permanent voucher specimens for pharmacognostic identification and authentication.
sections.scope: Applicable to Pharmacognosy laboratory and field collection activities for preparation of authenticated herbarium specimens from fresh medicinal plant collections.
procedure: Assemble the herbarium press: place one wooden lattice board flat on the floor or table.
Place 2–3 layers of newspaper followed by one sheet of blotting paper on the board.

Arrange the fresh plant specimen on the blotting paper — straighten leaves and stems to display all diagnostic features; show both upper and lower leaf surfaces (fold some leaves to expose undersurface).
Open flowers and fruits to show internal structures; use additional blotting paper strips to separate overlapping parts.
If the specimen is too long (> 42 cm), fold in a V or N shape.
Cover with another sheet of blotting paper and 2–3 layers of newspaper.
Add the next specimen layer repeating steps 3–6; the press can hold 20–30 specimens in a stack.
Place the second wooden lattice board on top of the stack.
Tighten the press straps or wingnut bolts firmly and evenly — compress until snug; do not over-tighten immediately.
Re-tighten after 2–4 hours as the compressed specimens relax.
Change the blotting paper daily for the first 3–4 days — this is the most critical step for rapid drying and mould prevention.
For succulent specimens: change blotting paper every 6–8 hours initially.
Drying is complete in 7–14 days when specimens are stiff, no longer cool to touch, and do not bend when lifted.
Carefully remove dried specimens and transfer to herbarium mounting.
Air-dry the press boards and blotting paper after use before storing.
precautions: Do not press wet or heavily succulent specimens without first blotting excess surface moisture — excessive moisture promotes rapid mould growth.
Change blotting paper frequently — leaving wet paper too long causes browning, mould, and specimen deterioration.
For very succulent plants (cactus, aloe): make incisions in thick parts before pressing to allow interior moisture to escape.
Label specimens with collection number immediately before pressing — labels placed after drying may be confused.
Keep pressed specimens away from insects — treat newly pressed specimens with insect repellent (naphthalene sachets placed in the press).
Do not over-tighten immediately — initial firm tightening is sufficient; re-tighten after first hour as specimens compress.
Inspect the press daily — address mould or insect infestation immediately to save specimens.
